Moore was associated with Dr. Foster in the publication of the Minnesotian prior to the consolidation, but when the offices separated it was stipulated that Mr. Moore should have the printing of the Journals of the two houses of the legislature as part payment of his share of the business of the late firm of Newson, Moore, Foster & Co., thus entirely severing his relations with the paper he helped to found.

s: St. Paul Press is founded by W. R. Marshall and Thomas F. Slaughter (using the Times office's material)
q: The Times continued under the management of Mr. Newson until the first of January, 1861, when he leased the office to W.R. Marshall and Thomas F. Slaughter, who started the St. Paul Daily Press with its material.

s: St. Paul Press acquires Minnesotian (the entire plant)
q: The Press proved to be too much of a competitor for the Minnesotian, and in a short time Dr. Foster was compelled to surrender to its enterprising projectors, they having purchased the entire plant.

s: St. Paul Press ends rivalry between Minnesotian and Times
q: This ended the rivalry between the two Republican dailies.

s: Daily North Star be an organ at the capital of the state (for Mr. Breckinridge's cause)
q: The supporters of Mr. Breckinridge thought their cause would present a more respectable appearance if they had an organ at the capital of the state. Accordingly the late H.H. Young, the editor of the Henderson Independent, was brought down from that village and the Daily North Star soon made its appearance.

s: Daily North Star be an organ at the capital of the state (for Mr. Breckinridge's cause)
q: Accordingly the late H.H. Young, the editor of the Henderson Independent, was brought down from that village and the Daily North Star soon made its appearance.

s: Daily North Star be an organ at the capital of the state
q: The supporters of Mr. Breckinridge thought their cause would present a more respectable appearance if they had an organ at the capital of the state.

s: Sons of Malta has lodge in St. Paul
q: Two or three members of the Pioneer editorial staff procured a charter from Pittesburg in 1858 and instituted a lodge in St. Paul.

s: Daily North Star collapses after election (when officeholders no longer contributed toward its support)
q: This paper was published regularly until after election, and as the returns indicated that the officeholders would not much longer contribute toward its support it soon collapsed.

s: Sons of Malta initiation is exposed in Harper’s Weekly (with numerous illustrations)
q: Mr. Penman was so highly Indignant at the manner in which he had been handled during the initiation that he immediately wrote an expose of the secret work, with numerous illustrations, and had it published in Harper's Weekly.

s: Sons of Malta has membership merchants, lawyers, doctors, printers, and half of the male population (in St. Paul)
q: Merchants, lawyers, doctors, printers, and in fact half of the male population, was soon enrolled in the membership of the order.

s: Sons of Malta uses Sons of Malta initiation (grand, gloomy and peculiar)
q: There was something so grand, gloomy and peculiar about the initiation that made it certain that as soon as one victim had run the gauntlet he would not be satisfied until another one had been procured.

s: Sons of Malta investigates candidates prospective members (the whole lodge acts as a committee of investigation)
q: When a candidate had been proposed for membership the whole lodge acted as a committee of investigation, and if it could be ascertained that he had ever been derelict in his dealings with his fellow men he was sure to be charged with it when being examined by the high priest in the secret chamber of the order--that is, the candidate supposed he was in a secret chamber from the manner in which he had to be questioned, but when the hood had been removed from his face he found, much to his mortification, that his confession had been made to the full membership of the order.

s: Sons of Malta originates bouncing candidates into the air from a rubber blanket (said to be original; one of the mildest atrocities)
q: The scheme of bouncing candidates into the air from a rubber blanket, so popular during the days of the recent ice carnivals was said to have been original with the Sons of Malta, and was one of the mildest of the many atrocities perpetrated by this most noble order.

s: Sons of Malta has headquarters in Empire Hall
q: The exposition acted like a bombshell in the camp of the Philistines, and ever after Empire hall, the headquarters of the order, presented a dark and gloomy appearance.

s: Sons of Malta has member John Penman
q: This organization kept on increasing in membership, until in an evil hour one of the members had succeeded in inducing the Rev. John Penman to consent to become one of its members.

s: The Great Sioux Outbreak in 1862 is a Indian warfare
q: It was during this critical period in the great struggle for the suppression of the Rebellion that one of the most fiendish atrocities in the history of Indian warfare was enacted on the western boundaries of Minnesota.

s: Sioux sell all their lands in Minnesota (except a strip ten miles wide on each side of the Minnesota river from near Fort Ridgely to Big Stone lake)
q: By the terms of the treaty of Traverse des Sioux and Mendota in 1851 the Sioux sold all their lands in Minnesota, except a strip ten miles wide on each side of the Minnesota river from near Fort Ridgely to Big Stone lake.

s: Treaty of Traverse des Sioux and Mendota transferred land from Sioux (in Minnesota, excepting the reserved strip)
q: By the terms of the treaty of Traverse des Sioux and Mendota in 1851 the Sioux sold all their lands in Minnesota, except a strip ten miles wide on each side of the Minnesota river from near Fort Ridgely to Big Stone lake.

s: Little Crow influenced Minnesota land sale (in 1858)
q: In 1858 ten miles of the strip lying north of the river was sold, mainly through the influence of Little Crow.

s: Little Crow was denounced by Sioux (for his role in selling the strip)
q: The selling of this strip caused great dissatisfaction among the Indians and Little Crow was severely denounced for the part he took in the transaction.

s: Sioux had grievances against traders (over accounts and annuity deductions)
q: The Indians also claimed that they were not fairly dealt with by the traders; that they had to rely entirely upon their word for their indebtedness to them; that they were ignorant of any method of keeping accounts, and that when the paymaster came the traders generally took all that was coming, and often leaving many of them in debt.

s: Sioux awaited Sioux annuity payment (for several weeks before the outbreak)
q: For several weeks previous to the outbreak the Indians came to the agencies to get their money. Day after day and week after week passed and there was no sign of paymasters.

s: United States government failed to make Sioux annuity payment (during the Civil War)
q: The Indians were told that on account of the great war in which the government was engaged the payment would never be made.

s: Sioux communicated with Hole-in-the-Day (before the outbreak)
q: It is known that the Sioux had been in communication with Hole-in-the-Day, the Chippewa chief, but the outbreak was probably precipitated before they came to an understanding.

s: The Great Sioux Outbreak in 1862 occurred in Minnesota (on the western boundaries)
q: It was during this critical period in the great struggle for the suppression of the Rebellion that one of the most fiendish atrocities in the history of Indian warfare was enacted on the western boundaries of Minnesota.

s: Sioux attacked Company B of the Fifth Regiment (by ambush near the scene of the revolt)
q: A detachment of Company B of the Fifth regiment, under command of Capt. Marsh, went to the scene of the revolt, but they were ambushed and about twenty-five of their number, including the captain, killed.

s: Other Day rescued Minnesota River refugees (sixty-two men, women and children)
q: Other Day, who piloted sixty-two men, women and children across the country from below Yellow Medicine to Kandiyohi, and from there to Hutchinson, Glencoe and Carver.

s: Other Day arrived at St. Paul (a few days after leading his party to safety)
q: Other Day arrived in St. Paul a few days after he had piloted his party in safety to Carver

s: Other Day attributed escape to Great Spirit (according to his statement in St. Paul)
q: I attribute it to the mercy of the Great Spirit.

s: Henry Hastings Sibley be placed in command of the troops (ordered to assemble at St. Peter)
q: Ex-Gov. Sibley, on account of his long familiarity with Indian character, was placed in command of the troops ordered to assemble at St. Peter, and in a few days, with detachments of the regiments then forming, half-uniformed, poorly armed and with a scant supply of ammunition, commenced offensive operations against the murderous redskins.

s: Fort Ridgely was besieged by Sioux (about 700 or 800 armed warriors for several days)
q: He was surrounded by 700 or 800 Sioux, fully armed and equipped. Although there were only two attempts made to capture the garrison by assault, yet the siege was kept up for several days.

s: Fort Ridgely was defended by Lieut. T. J. Sheehan (with about 150 Fifth Regiment men, 50 Renville Rangers and civilians)
q: The garrison was under the command of Lieut. T.J. Sheehan. His force consisted of about 150 men from the Fifth regiment, fifty men of the Renville Rangers, and a number of civilians.

s: Fort Ridgely was relieved by Henry Hastings Sibley (after more than a week of defense)
q: After bravely defending the fort for more than a week, the little garrison was relieved by the arrival of about 200 mounted volunteers under command of Col. McPhail, being the advance of Gen. Sibley's command.

s: The Great Sioux Outbreak in 1862 began on 1862-08-18 (without warning)
q: On the morning of the 18th of August, without a word of warning, an indiscriminate massacre was inaugurated.

s: New Ulm appear in the vicinity of New Ulm (with the evident intention of burning and pillaging the village)
q: Almost simultaneously with the attack on Fort Ridgely the Indians in large numbers appeared in the vicinity of New Ulm, with the evident intention of burning and pillaging the village.

s: Charles E. Flandrau organize a company of volunteers (to the relief of that place)
q: Judge Charles E. Flandrau of this city, who was then residing at St. Peter, organized a company of volunteers and marched across the country to the relief of that place.

s: Charles E. Flandrau evacuated New Ulm evacuation (after provisions and ammunition became scarce)
q: Provisions and ammunition becoming scarce, the judge decided to evacuate the town and march across the country to Mankato.

s: New Ulm evacuation ended at Mankato (with women, children and wounded men in about 150 wagons)
q: They made up a train of about 150 wagons, loaded them with women and children and the men who had been wounded in the fight, and arrived safely in Mankato without being molested.

s: Birch Coulie battle was fought by Maj. Joseph R. Brown (with about 150 men, including St. Paul volunteers)
q: Maj. Brown had about one hundred and fifty men under his command. About 4 o'clock on the following morning the Indians, to the number of 500 or 600, well armed and most of them mounted, commenced an indiscriminate fire upon the almost helpless little command.

s: Birch Coulie battle lasted two days (until relief arrived)
q: For two days they bravely defended themselves, and when relief finally arrived it was found that about half their number had been killed or wounded.

s: St. Paul felt safe after Battle of Wood Lake (from raids by the hostile Sioux)
q: it was not until after the battle of Wood Lake that the people of St. Paul felt that they were perfectly safe from raids by the hostile Sioux.

s: The Great Sioux Outbreak in 1862 caused Sioux massacre (throughout the Sioux reservation)
q: The horrible work of murder, pillage and destruction was spread throughout the entire Sioux reservation, and whole families, especially those in isolated portions of the country, were an easy prey to these fiendish warriors.

s: The Great Sioux Outbreak in 1862 rendered homeless 30000 people (in less than one week)
q: In less than one week 1,000 people had been killed, several million dollars' worth of property destroyed and 30,000 people rendered homeless.

s: United States government was engaged in Civil War (in 1862)
q: The year 1862 was the the second year of the great Rebellion, and as the government officers had been taxed to their utmost to provide funds for the prosecution of the war, it looked as though they had neglected their wards in Minnesota.

s: Abraham Lincoln issued 600,000-volunteer enlistment (in July and August 1862)
q: In July and August, 1862, President Lincoln issued proclamations calling for the enlistment of 600,000 volunteers for the purpose of reinforcing the army, then vainly endeavoring to suppress the Southern rebellion.

s: 600,000-volunteer enlistment supported United States government (for reinforcing the army)
q: President Lincoln issued proclamations calling for the enlistment of 600,000 volunteers for the purpose of reinforcing the army, then vainly endeavoring to suppress the Southern rebellion.

s: Minnesota was called upon to furnish Minnesota regiments (under the presidential call for 600,000 men)
q: Under the call of the president for 600,000 men Minnesota was called upon to furnish five regiments--the Sixth, Seventh, Eighth, Ninth and Tenth--and the requisition had been partially filled and the men mustered in when the news reached St. Paul that open hostilities had commenced at the upper agency, and an indiscriminate massacre of the whites was taking place.

s: Henry Hastings Sibley commands expedition (about 2,000 men and a battery)
q: As soon as Gen. Sibley had collected a sufficient force to enable him to move with safety he decided upon offensive operations. He had collected about 2,000 men from the regiments then forming, including the Third regiment, recently paroled, and a battery under command of Capt. Mark Hendricks.

s: The Great Sioux Outbreak in 1862 is declared over by Gen. Pope (after the Wood Lake battle)
q: After the battle Gen. Pope, who was in command of the department of the Northwest, telegraphed the war department that the Indian war was over and asked what disposition to make of the troops then under his command.

s: Minnesota opposes removal of troops (through public remonstrance)
q: This request of Gen. Pope was met with a decided remonstrance by the people of Minnesota, and they succeeded in preventing the removal of any of the troops until they had made two long marches through the Dakotas and to Montana.

s: Indian camp at Camp Release contains mixed bloods and white women and children (about 250 captives)
q: They had with them about two hundred and fifty mixed bloods and white women and children, and the soldiers were very anxious to precede at once to their rescue.

s: mixed bloods and white women and children are released at Camp Release (after the entire camp surrendered)
q: After a few preliminary consultations the entire camp surrendered and the captives were released.

s: military tribunal convicts condemned Indians (321 defendants found guilty)
q: After a series of sittings, lasting from the 30th of September to the 5th of November, 321 of the fiends were found guilty of the offenses charged, 303 of whom were sentenced to death and the rest condemned to various terms of imprisonment according to their crimes.

s: condemned Indians are confined at Mankato (in a large jail)
q: All of the condemned prisoners were taken to Mankato and were confined in a large jail constructed for the purpose.

s: Abraham Lincoln limits execution of condemned Indians (to thirty-eight of the most flagrant cases)
q: The president, after consulting his military advisers, decided to permit the execution of only thirty-eight of the most flagrant cases, and accordingly directed them to be hung on the 26th of December, 1862.

s: Quakers of Philadelphia remonstrate with Abraham Lincoln (against the proposed executions)
q: The Quakers of Philadelphia and the good people of Massachusetts sent many remonstrances to the president to put a stop to the proposed wholesale execution.

s: execution of the thirty-eight Dakota prisoners be directed to occur on the 26th of December, 1862
q: The president, after consulting his military advisers, decided to permit the execution of only thirty-eight of the most flagrant cases, and accordingly directed them to be hung on the 26th of December, 1862.

s: Rev. S.R. Riggs interviews condemned Indians (before their execution)
q: Previous to their execution the condemned prisoners were interviewed by Rev. S.R. Riggs, to whom they made their dying confessions.

s: Henry Hastings Sibley reaches Camp Release (on September 26)
q: Gen. Sibley's command reached Camp Release on the 26th of September, in the vicinity of which was located a large camp of Indians, most of whom had been engaged in the massacres.

s: Little Crow leads The Great Sioux Outbreak in 1862 (acknowledged head of the war party)
q: Although greatly disliked by many of the Indians, he was the acknowledged head of the war party and by common consent assumed the direction of all the hostile tribes in their fruitless struggle against the whites.

s: Little Crow is born at Kaposia (a few miles below St. Paul)
q: Little Crow was born in Kaposia, a few miles below St. Paul, and was always known as a bad Indian.

s: Little Crow is killed by Lamson (near Hutchinson after escaping surrender)
q: Little Crow, the chief instigator of the insurrection was not with the number that surrendered, but escaped and was afterward killed by a farmer named Lamson, in the vicinity of Hutchinson.

s: Little Crow is held by Minnesota Historical Society (his scalp is preserved there)
q: His scalp is now in the state historical society.

s: condemned Indians are transferred to Davenport (the balance of those not executed)
q: The balance of the condemned were kept in close confinement till spring, when they were taken to Davenport, and afterward to some point on the Missouri river

s: Henry Hastings Sibley forms military tribunal (to try suspected offenders)
q: As soon as possible Gen. Sibley made inquiries as to the participation of these Indians in the terrible crimes recently perpetrated, and it soon developed that a large number of them had been guilty of the grossest atrocities. The general decided to form a military tribunal and try the offenders.

s: transportation of military supplies uses wagon (because there were no railroads)
q: One of the most perplexing problems the military authorities had to contend with was the transportation of supplies to the troops on the frontier. There were, of course, no railroads, and the only way to transport provisions was by wagon.

s: Company K of the Eighth regiment is sent transportation of military supplies (on that especial duty)
q: A detachment of Company K of the Eighth regiment was sent down from the fort and remained in the city several days on that especial duty.

s: Ladies Aid Society meets at Ingersoll Hall (for sewing and relief work)
q: Ladies Aid Society--A meeting of the ladies' aid society for the purpose of sewing for the relief of the wounded soldiers at our forts, and also for the assistance of the destitute refugees now thronging our city, is called to meet this morning at Ingersoll hall.

s: Mrs. Stella Selby is president of Ladies Aid Society
q: By order of the president, "Mrs. Stella Selby. "Miss M.O. Holyoke, Secretary."

s: Miss M.O. Holyoke is secretary of Ladies Aid Society
q: By order of the president, "Mrs. Stella Selby. "Miss M.O. Holyoke, Secretary."

s: Dakota lands in Minnesota is forfeited to the government (by reason of the outbreak; about 750,000 acres)
q: By reason of the outbreak the Sioux forfeited to the government, in addition to an annual annuity of $68,000 for fifty years, all the lands they held in Minnesota, amounting in the aggregate to about 750,000 acres, worth at the present time something like $15,000,000.

s: Battle of Wood Lake is a battle (the only real battle of the war)
q: This was the only real battle of the war.

s: Dakota lands in Minnesota has associated annuity annual annuity ($68,000 for fifty years)
q: By reason of the outbreak the Sioux forfeited to the government, in addition to an annual annuity of $68,000 for fifty years, all the lands they held in Minnesota, amounting in the aggregate to about 750,000 acres, worth at the present time something like $15,000,000.

s: Battle of Wood Lake opposes Sioux (about 800 soldiers against about an equal number of Indians)
q: About 800 of the command were engaged in the encounter and were opposed by about an equal number of Indians.

s: Sioux are routed in Battle of Wood Lake (by Col. Marshall's charge)
q: After a spirited engagement Col. Marshall, with about 400 men, made a double-quick charge upon the Sioux and succeeded in utterly routing them.

s: Other Day supports Henry Hastings Sibley (fights with the whites)
q: Other Day was with the whites and took a conspicuous part in the encounter.

s: firemen and fires of pioneer days is a brief history
q: FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS. A BRIEF HISTORY OF THE ST. PAUL, FIRE DEPARTMENT--PIONEER HOOK AND LADDER COMPANY--HOPE ENGINE COMPANY AND MINNEHAHA ENGINE COMPANY--A LARGE NUMBER OF HOTEL FIRES.

s: St. Paul requires firefighting equipment (building owners were required to provide marked buckets)
q: In the fall of 1850 the town fathers of St. Paul passed an ordinance requiring the owners of all buildings, public or private, to provide and keep in good repair, substantial buckets, marked with paint the word "Fire" on one side and the owner's name on the other, subject to inspection by the fire warden and to be under his control when occasion required.

s: R.C. Knox organizes fire brigade (first attempt in St. Paul)
q: The first attempt at organizing a fire brigade, was made by R.C. Knox in the fall of 1851.

s: R.C. Knox purchases ladders (with money raised by subscription)
q: Mr. Knox raised a small sum of money by subscription, with which he purchased several ladders, and they were frequently brought into requisition by the little band of men whom Mr. Knox had associated with him.

s: John McCloud purchases first fire engine introduced in the Northwest (jointly with Thompson Ritchie and at their own expense)
q: Two public-spirited citizens of St. Paul, John McCloud and Thompson Ritchie, purchased in the East and brought to the city at their own expense the first fire engine introduced in the Northwest.

s: John McCloud is a hardware dealer (member of McCloud & Bro.)
q: Mr. McCloud was a member of the firm of McCloud & Bro., hardware dealers, and they occupied the building on the southwest corner of Third and Cedar streets.

s: Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1 is organized under provisions of the city charter
q: In November, 1854, Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1 was organized under provisions of the city charter.

s: Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1 owns truck (in 1856)
q: At that time they possessed one truck, hooks and ladders, and one fire engine with hose.
